title: Jira vs Plane
comparison_markdown:
# Jira vs Plane (2026)

## Overview
Jira and Plane are two project management tools that help teams organize and track their work. This comparison is useful for teams currently using Jira who are considering switching to Plane, possibly due to the desire for more control over their data or to reduce costs. The core use case for both tools is issue tracking and project management, and someone would switch from Jira to Plane to gain more flexibility and autonomy over their project management system.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Jira is a paid service, while Plane is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: With Plane, teams have full control over their data, whereas Jira stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Plane requires more technical expertise to set up, whereas Jira offers a more straightforward onboarding process.
* Scalability: Jira is designed to handle large, complex projects, while Plane is better suited for smaller to medium-sized teams.
* Integration with Git: Jira has native integration with Git, while Plane relies on third-party integrations for version control.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Jira | Plane |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.75-$14.50/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $387.50-$725/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,550-$2,900/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Jira
* Robust set of features for project management
* Native integration with Git and other Atlassian tools
* Scalable and reliable infrastructure
* User-friendly interface
* Extensive customer support
### Plane
* Free and self-hosted, reducing costs
* Full control over data and security
* Customizable and flexible
* Open-source community support
* Lightweight and easy to use
However, Plane has limitations, including:
* Requires technical expertise to set up and maintain
* Limited native integrations with other tools
* Smaller user community compared to Jira

## When to Choose Each
Jira is the better choice for large, complex projects that require a robust set of features and native integrations with other tools. It is well-suited for teams with the budget to support its costs and the need for scalable, reliable infrastructure. On the other hand, Plane is ideal for smaller to medium-sized teams that value flexibility, autonomy, and cost-effectiveness. It is a good choice for teams with technical expertise and the ability to self-host and maintain their own project management system.

## Migration Path
1. Export Jira data in CSV or JSON format.
2. Use a third-party import tool, such as the Plane import script, to migrate data to Plane.
3. Configure Plane to match the team's workflow and needs.
4. Test the migration to ensure all data is correctly imported and functional.
5. Train team members on using Plane and its features.

## Our Take
Plane is not yet production-ready for most users, as it requires technical expertise to set up and maintain. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Plane relies on third-party integrations for version control, which may not be as seamless as Jira's native integration with Git. However, for teams that value flexibility, autonomy, and cost-effectiveness, and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and maintaining their own project management system, Plane is a viable alternative to Jira.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that do not need native Git integration
* Teams with technical expertise and the ability to self-host and maintain their own project management system
* Organizations with tight budgets that cannot afford Jira's costs
* Teams that value flexibility and autonomy over their project management system
* Teams with simple project management needs that do not require a robust set of features

## FAQ
### Is Plane free?
Yes, Plane is free and self-hosted, reducing costs for teams.
### Can I migrate my Jira data to Plane?
Yes, you can export Jira data in CSV or JSON format and use a third-party import tool to migrate it to Plane.
### Does Plane have native integration with Git?
No, Plane relies on third-party integrations for version control.
### Is Plane suitable for large, complex projects?
No, Plane is better suited for smaller to medium-sized teams and projects.
### Can I customize Plane to fit my team's workflow?
Yes, Plane is customizable and flexible, allowing teams to tailor it to their specific needs.

title: Trello vs WeKan
comparison_markdown:
# Trello vs WeKan

## Overview

Trello is a visual kanban board tool from Atlassian, simple and beginner-friendly. WeKan is an open-source kanban board offering the same card/list/board model without vendor dependency.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Trello paid plans start at $5/user/month; WeKan is completely free
- **Data control**: WeKan runs on your own server; Trello data lives on Atlassian infrastructure
- **Features**: Trello has a larger Power-Ups marketplace; WeKan covers core kanban features
- **Setup**: Trello requires zero setup; WeKan requires a server
- **Customization**: WeKan open-source code can be extended; Trello cannot

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Trello | WeKan |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $5+/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Trello

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### WeKan

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [wekan/wekan](https://github.com/wekan/wekan) * ~20k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Trello if:** Trello suits individuals and small teams wanting instant zero-setup kanban with integrations to Slack, Google Drive, and GitHub.

**Choose WeKan if:** WeKan is ideal for teams wanting full data ownership or air-gapped deployments.

## Migration Path

Export Trello boards as JSON, then use WeKan Trello importer in Settings to recreate boards, lists, and cards.

## Our Take

WeKan is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Trello tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your WeKan instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Trello, switching to self-hosted WeKan will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Trello until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Trello paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is WeKan free to use?
Yes. WeKan is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Trello to WeKan?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Trello data, follow the WeKan import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does WeKan get regular updates?
Yes. WeKan has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use WeKan without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if WeKan development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced July 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Trello](https://trello.com) and [WeKan](https://wekan.github.io) before making decisions.*

title: Dropbox vs Nextcloud
comparison_markdown:
# Dropbox vs Nextcloud (2026)

## Overview
Dropbox and Nextcloud are cloud storage solutions that enable users to store and share files. This comparison is beneficial for individuals and teams seeking to manage their data efficiently, with a key reason to switch being the desire for greater control over data ownership and security. The core use case for both tools is file storage and collaboration, with the main difference lying in their approach to data ownership and hosting.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Dropbox offers a paid subscription model, while Nextcloud is free and open-source, allowing for self-hosting.
* Data ownership: Nextcloud prioritizes user data ownership, whereas Dropbox's terms and conditions grant the company certain rights to user data.
* Setup complexity: Nextcloud requires more technical expertise for setup, especially for self-hosting, compared to Dropbox's straightforward sign-up process.
* Scalability: Nextcloud is highly scalable, especially when self-hosted, as users can choose their own infrastructure, whereas Dropbox has predefined storage limits.
* Integration with calendar: Nextcloud offers a native calendar app, whereas Dropbox relies on third-party integrations for similar functionality.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Dropbox | Nextcloud |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $9.99-$16.58/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $9.99-$16.58/user/month (approximately $499.50-$829/month) | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $9.99-$16.58/user/month (approximately $1,998-$3,316/month) | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Dropbox:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Wide range of integrations with third-party apps
* Robust security features
* Good customer support
* Limited control over data ownership
**Nextcloud:**
* High degree of control over data ownership and security
* Self-hosting option for greater flexibility
* Open-source and free
* Integrates well with other open-source tools
* Can be complex to set up and manage, especially for non-technical users

## When to Choose Each
When choosing Dropbox, consider teams that prioritize ease of use and have fewer concerns about data ownership. Dropbox is suitable for small to medium-sized teams that need a straightforward, user-friendly cloud storage solution with a wide range of integrations. On the other hand, Nextcloud is ideal for teams that value data security and ownership, such as large enterprises or organizations handling sensitive information. Nextcloud's self-hosting option and open-source nature make it an attractive choice for teams with the technical expertise to manage their own infrastructure.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Dropbox data using the Dropbox export tool, which provides a ZIP archive of your files.
2. Set up a Nextcloud instance, either self-hosted or through a provider.
3. Use the Nextcloud WebDAV interface to import your Dropbox data, or utilize a third-party migration tool for a more streamlined process.

## Our Take
Nextcloud is not yet production-ready for most users due to its complexity and the technical expertise required for setup and management. One specific technical limitation worth noting is Nextcloud's limited support for certain file types and integrations, which may hinder its adoption in certain environments. However, for teams prioritizing data ownership and security, Nextcloud is a viable alternative to Dropbox, and we recommend considering it for self-hosting or through a trusted provider.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that do not need advanced collaboration features and prioritize data ownership.
* Medium-sized teams (10-50 users) that require high security and are willing to manage their own infrastructure.
* Large enterprises (over 50 users) that handle sensitive data and need complete control over their cloud storage.
* Teams that do not require seamless integration with Microsoft Office tools.
* Organizations with existing Linux infrastructure that can easily integrate Nextcloud.

## FAQ
### Can I use Nextcloud for free?
Yes, Nextcloud is free and open-source, allowing for self-hosting and customization. However, self-hosting requires technical expertise and infrastructure costs.
### Is Nextcloud more secure than Dropbox?
Nextcloud prioritizes user data ownership and security, offering end-to-end encryption and granular access controls, making it a more secure option for sensitive data.
### Can I migrate my Dropbox data to Nextcloud directly?
While there is no direct migration tool, you can export your Dropbox data and import it into Nextcloud using the WebDAV interface or third-party migration tools.
### Does Nextcloud support real-time collaboration?
Nextcloud offers real-time collaboration features, including document editing and commenting, but these features may not be as polished as those offered by Dropbox.
### Is Nextcloud suitable for personal use?
Yes, Nextcloud can be used for personal cloud storage, especially for individuals prioritizing data ownership and security, but it may require more technical expertise to set up and manage.
meta_description: Nextcloud, a free self-hosted cloud storage solution, offers greater control over data ownership and security, see full comparison or free migration guide.

# Linear vs Plane (2026)

* Scalability: Linear is designed to scale with large teams and enterprises, while Plane's scalability depends on the server infrastructure used for self-hosting.
* Integration difference: Linear has a more comprehensive set of integrations with third-party tools, including popular services like GitHub and Slack, whereas Plane's integrations are more limited but can be extended through its API.

### Linear
* Easy to set up and use
* Comprehensive integrations with third-party tools
* Scalable for large teams and enterprises
* User-friendly interface
* Limited control over data storage and security
### Plane
* Free and self-hosted
* Full control over data storage and security
* Customizable through API and extensions
* Limited integrations with third-party tools
* Requires technical expertise for setup and maintenance

On the other hand, Plane is perfect for small to medium-sized teams or organizations that value data ownership, customization, and cost-effectiveness. ## Who Should Switch

* Teams that require full control over their data storage and security
* Organizations with limited budgets that can't afford Linear's per-user cost
* Development teams that can handle the technical setup and maintenance of a self-hosted solution
* Teams that prioritize customization and flexibility in their project management tool

No, Plane's interface is more geared towards developers and technical teams, and may not be as user-friendly as Linear's.

Yes, Plane is highly customizable through its API and extensions, allowing teams to tailor the tool to their specific needs.

# Google Workspace vs Nextcloud (2026)

## Overview
Google Workspace and Nextcloud are two popular productivity and collaboration platforms that cater to different needs and use cases. The core use case for both tools is to facilitate team collaboration and productivity, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

* Cost: Google Workspace charges a monthly fee per user, while Nextcloud is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: Google Workspace stores data on its servers, while Nextcloud allows users to host their data on their own servers.
* Setup complexity: Google Workspace is generally easier to set up, while Nextcloud requires more technical expertise.
* Scalability: Google Workspace is highly scalable, while Nextcloud's scalability depends on the user's server infrastructure.
* Integration: Google Workspace integrates seamlessly with other Google apps, while Nextcloud offers integration with a range of third-party apps through its API.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Google Workspace | Nextcloud |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $6-$18/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $300-$900/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,200-$3,600/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Google Workspace:**
* Easy to set up and use
* Highly scalable
* Integrates well with other Google apps
* Offers a range of collaboration features
* Reliable customer support
* Limited control over data storage and security
**Nextcloud:**
* Free and self-hosted
* Offers high level of control over data storage and security
* Highly customizable
* Integrates with a range of third-party apps
* Can be more cost-effective for large teams
* Requires technical expertise to set up and maintain
* Limited customer support

## When to Choose Each
Google Workspace is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams that need a easy-to-use and scalable collaboration platform. It's ideal for teams that are already using other Google apps and want to integrate them seamlessly. On the other hand, Nextcloud is a good choice for larger teams or organizations that want to have more control over their data and security. It's ideal for teams that have the technical expertise to set up and maintain their own servers.

Nextcloud is suitable for teams that value data sovereignty and want to avoid vendor lock-in. It's also a good choice for teams that want to customize their collaboration platform to meet their specific needs. However, it may not be the best choice for small teams or teams that don't have the technical expertise to set up and maintain their own servers.

1. Export your data from Google Workspace using the Google Takeout tool, which exports data in a ZIP file.

4. Configure your Nextcloud instance to integrate with any third-party apps you need.

## Our Take
Nextcloud is a production-ready platform for most users, but it may require some technical expertise to set up and maintain. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Nextcloud's scalability depends on the user's server infrastructure, which can be a challenge for large teams. However, for teams that value data sovereignty and want to avoid vendor lock-in, Nextcloud is a good choice.

Nextcloud's community is active and supportive, which can be helpful for teams that need assistance with setup and maintenance. Additionally, Nextcloud's API makes it easy to integrate with a range of third-party apps, which can be useful for teams that need to customize their collaboration platform.

Overall, we recommend Nextcloud for teams that value data sovereignty and want to avoid vendor lock-in. However, for small teams or teams that don't have the technical expertise to set up and maintain their own servers, Google Workspace may be a better choice.

## Who Should Switch
* Large teams (100+ users) that want to reduce costs and have more control over their data
* Teams that value data sovereignty and want to avoid vendor lock-in
* Organizations that require high levels of security and compliance
* Teams that need to customize their collaboration platform to meet their specific needs
* Teams that don't need the full range of Google apps and want a more streamlined collaboration platform
